title: Generics from zero: type parameters
goal: By the end you can write generic classes and functions in Kotlin and Java, read `<T>` as a blank the caller fills in, and explain why a type parameter moves a ClassCastException from the read to a compile error at the write.

warmup.q: A `MutableList<Any>` holds payment ids. One module adds the `Int` 1001 by mistake. Much later another module runs `val id = ids[0] as String`. Where do you first hear about the bug?
options: A compile error on the line that adds 1001
An exception on the line that adds 1001
A ClassCastException on the `as String` line in the other module
warmup.why: An `Int` is an `Any`, so the add compiles and runs. The cast is the only check, and it runs in the reader. The exception names the reader's line, not the line with the bug. A `MutableList<String>` would have stopped the add at compile time.

sections.h: Inference fills in most type arguments for you
sections.body:
You rarely write type arguments in Kotlin. The compiler works them out from the values you pass. This is **type inference**, and Java does it too, with `var` and the diamond.

```java
var amounts = List.of(1200, 350, 99);            // List<Integer>
var box = new Box<>("EUR");                      // Box<String>
var fees = Map.of("EUR", 100, "USD", 250L);      // Map<String, Number & Comparable<...> & ...>
```

```kotlin
val amounts = listOf(1200, 350, 99)              // List<Int>
val box = Box("EUR")                             // Box<String>
val fees = mapOf("EUR" to 100, "USD" to 250L)    // Map<String, Long>
```

Look at the last line in each. Kotlin sees `250L` in the same map and makes the literal `100` a `Long`, so both values fit `Long`. Java never changes a literal's type: `100` stays an `Integer`, and javac infers a long intersection type for the values instead.

When the values really have different types, the compiler picks the closest type they share:

```java
var mixed = List.of(1, 2.5);     // List<Number & Comparable<...> & Constable & ConstantDesc>
var odd = List.of(1, "a");       // another intersection, of Serializable, Comparable and more
```

```kotlin
val mixed = listOf(1, 2.5)       // List<Number & Comparable<*>>
val odd = listOf(1, "a")         // List<Comparable<*> & Serializable>
```

`Number & Comparable<*>` is an **intersection type**: something that is both a `Number` and a `Comparable`. You cannot write that type in your own code, but the compiler uses it. When you see one, you have usually mixed types by accident.

Sometimes there is nothing to infer from. `emptyList()` gets no values, so Kotlin has no clue what `T` should be:

```text
error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly.
```

Java does not complain here. `var none = Collections.emptyList();` quietly becomes a `List<Object>`, which is rarely what you meant. In both languages the fix is the same. Write the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let the compiler work backwards from it:

```java
var none = Collections.<String>emptyList();
List<String> alsoNone = Collections.emptyList();
```

```kotlin
val none = emptyList<String>()
val alsoNone: List<String> = emptyList()
```

Each pair means the same thing. I use the first form inside expressions and the second for properties, where the declared type documents the API anyway.

Kotlin builders infer too. `buildList { add("idem_1"); add("idem_2") }` is a `List<String>`, worked out from the `add` calls inside the lambda. Java has no such builder, so there you name the type up front: `new ArrayList<String>()`.

Here is a trick you will use for the rest of this track. When you are not sure what the compiler inferred, assign the value to a type you know is wrong, such as `val probe: Int = mixed` in Kotlin or `int probe = mixed;` in Java. The error message prints the real type.

try.expect: Gradle prints `Note: ... RawTypeDemo.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations.` The program prints `size = 2, nothing failed yet` and `PAY_1001`, then a `ClassCastException` for the `Integer`. The add worked; the failure comes in the loop, where javac inserted a hidden cast to `String`. With `List<String> ids` the build fails at `ids.add(42)` with `incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String`.

analogy: An `Any` box is an unlabeled crate in a warehouse. Anyone can put anything in it, and you find out what is inside when you open it at the far end of the building. A `Box<String>` is a crate with a label, and the loading dock refuses anything that does not match the label. You stop the wrong item at the door instead of at the other end. The analogy breaks in one place: a real label travels with the crate. On the JVM the label is removed after the loading dock, so the check happens at compile time only and the running program cannot read it.
in_your_world: Payment services collect untyped bags: a `Map<String, Any>` of payment metadata, Kafka record headers read as bytes, a JSON blob from the card issuer parsed into a map. Every `as String` or `as Long` on a read is a place where a `ClassCastException` can show up far from the code that wrote the value. When you own the type, give it a type parameter or a real class (`data class PaymentMetadata(val merchantId: String, val retries: Int)`). When you do not own it, convert once at the edge, in the Kafka deserializer or the HTTP client, so everything behind that line is typed. The Kafka client already does this for you: a `ConsumerRecord<String, PaymentEvent>` hands you a typed value.
mistake: The common mistake is choosing `Any` or `Map<String, Any>` "to keep it flexible" and casting on every read. People do it because it compiles, and the first version has one writer and one reader who agree. Six months later there are five writers, and one of them stores an `Int`. The fix is to put the type in the signature: a type parameter when the content varies (`Box<T>`, `Cache<V>`), or a small typed class when the shape is fixed. If the values really are of several kinds, use a sealed interface, not `Any`.

compare.title: One generic box and one generic function, in both languages

java.title: Box.java

kotlin.title: Box.kt

compare.note: The model is the same: one class, type parameters checked at compile time, one runtime class. Kotlin infers the type argument from constructor arguments without a diamond, and it has no raw types, so the unchecked-warning escape hatch that Java keeps for old code does not exist. Kotlin also accepts `Int` as a type argument, while Java forces you to write `Integer`. Both compile to boxed objects. One more difference shows in `firstOrNull`: Kotlin's return type says `T?`, so callers must handle null. Java's `T` can be null without saying so.

steps.say: A payment API caches the response for each idempotency key, so a retried request gets the same answer. The first version stores `Any`, and every caller casts. Find the two places a wrong type could get in or out.

1. Decide what varies. The key is always a `String`. The response type changes per endpoint: authorizations, refunds, captures. So the response type becomes the type parameter, and the key stays a plain `String`.
2. Fill the blank at the use site. Each endpoint gets its own cache with its own type. The cast is gone, and a wrong put is now a compile error.

3. Add a helper that computes on a miss. It uses the class's `R`, so it needs no `<R>` of its own. Stop and answer: what would go wrong if you wrote `fun <R> getOrPut(...)` here? (A new `R` on the function would hide the class's `R`, and `responses[key] = value` would no longer type-check. The same happens in Java with `<R> R getOrPut(...)`.)

lab.title: Write a generic Stack, two generic functions and a Duo
steps: Run the tests once. All nine fail with `NotImplementedError`.
In `Stack.kt`, add a `private val items = mutableListOf<T>()` and write the five members. `pop` on an empty stack throws `NoSuchElementException`.
In `Search.kt`, write `firstMatching` with a plain `for` loop, then `indexBy`. `indexBy` keeps the first item it sees for each key.
In `Duo.kt`, write `swap`, `mapSecond` and `zipToDuos`. Read each return type first: it tells you what to build.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then search your code for `as `: there should be no casts at all.
hints: For `indexBy`, a `LinkedHashMap<K, T>` with `putIfAbsent(key(item), item)` keeps the first item and the input order.
`swap()` is one line: `Duo(second, first)`. The compiler checks that it is a `Duo<B, A>`.
lab.done_when: All nine tests in `GenericsFromZeroTest` pass, and your code has no `as` casts.

drill.title: Write Box and firstOrNull from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In a scratch file, write a `Box<T>` class with a value and a `replace` method that returns the old value, plus a generic `lastOrNull(items)` function. Write it in Kotlin, then in Java. Check: where did each `<T>` go?

alt.title: Box.java

recap: A cast from `Any` checks the type late, at the read, so the exception points at the reader and not at the bug.
`class Box<T>` declares a type parameter. `Box<String>` fills it with a type argument, and the compiler checks every use.
Kotlin puts a function's `<T>` before the name (`fun <T> f`). Java puts it before the return type (`static <T> T f`).
Inference fills in most type arguments. When there is nothing to infer from, write `emptyList<String>()` or declare the variable's type.
Assign a value to a wrong type (`val probe: Int = x`) to make the compiler print what it inferred.
Java raw types (`List` with no `<...>`) switch the checks off. Kotlin has none.

quiz.q: Payment metadata is a `MutableMap<String, Any>`. A retry handler stores `meta["retries"] = "3"`. A report later runs `val n = meta["retries"] as Int`. What happens?
options: A compile error on the line that stores "3"
A ClassCastException on the line that stores "3"
A ClassCastException on the `as Int` line, when the report runs
`n` is 3, because Kotlin converts the string
quiz.why: A `String` is an `Any`, so the store compiles and runs. The cast in the report is the first check, and it fails there. Casts never convert values. A typed field such as `retries: Int` would have made the store a compile error.

quiz.q: Given `fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T?`, what does the compiler say about `val id: String? = firstOrNull(listOf(1, 2))`?
quiz.why: `T` is inferred from the argument as `Int`, so the call returns `Int?`. That does not fit in a `String?`. The type parameter ties the input and the output together, which is the whole point. Nothing is converted at run time.

quiz.q: `val none = emptyList()` does not compile. Which line fixes it?
quiz.why: The compiler needs to know `T`. You can give the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let inference work backwards from it. Both produce a `List<String>`.

quiz.q: Java: `List raw = new ArrayList(); raw.add(7); List<String> names = raw; String s = names.get(0);` What happens?
options: It compiles with unchecked warnings, then throws ClassCastException on the `names.get(0)` line
quiz.why: Raw types turn the checks off, so javac only warns. The `Integer` sits in the list until the read, where javac inserted a cast to `String`. The failure appears far from the line that caused it, the same as with `Any`.

quiz.q: From the race conditions lesson: a Kafka consumer does `if (!seen.contains(key)) { charge(m); seen.add(key) }`, where `seen` is `ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>()`. Two copies of one message arrive on two threads. What is the smallest fix?
options: Call `charge` only after `seen.add(key)` returned true: `if (seen.add(key)) charge(m)`
Make `seen` a `MutableSet<Any>` so both copies fit
quiz.why: This is check-then-act. Each set call is atomic, but two calls in a row are not. `add` checks and inserts in one step and returns false for the second copy, so only one thread charges. `volatile` and a synchronized wrapper leave the gap between the two calls.

flashcards.back: A type parameter: a blank that each user of `Box` fills with a real type, such as `Box<String>`.

flashcards.front: Where does a bad value stored in an `Any` field get caught?
flashcards.back: At the cast in the code that reads it, at run time. The stack trace points at the reader, not at the writer with the bug.
`cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly.` Fix: `emptyList<String>()` or `val e: List<String> = emptyList()`.

flashcards.front: Where does `<T>` go in a Kotlin generic function, and in a Java one?
flashcards.back: Kotlin: before the name, `fun <T> first(xs: List<T>): T`. Java: before the return type, `static <T> T first(List<T> xs)`.

flashcards.front: What does Java's diamond in `new ArrayList<>()` do?
flashcards.back: It tells javac to infer the type argument from the target type. Without it, `new ArrayList()` is a raw type.
`List<Number & Comparable<*>>`, an intersection type: the closest type that both `Int` and `Double` share.

flashcards.front: How do you see the type Kotlin inferred for `x`?
flashcards.back: Write `val probe: Int = x`. The compile error prints the actual type.

terms.plain: The placeholder in a declaration, like `T` in `class Box<T>`.
The real type that fills a type parameter, like `String` in `Box<String>`.
A function with its own type parameters, such as `fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T?`.
The compiler working out type arguments from the values and the expected type.
A type that is two types at once, like `Number & Comparable<*>`. Inferred by the compiler; you cannot write it yourself.
Java's `<>` on `new`, asking javac to infer the type arguments.
A Java generic type used without type arguments, like plain `List`. The compiler stops checking it.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to keep a `Map<String, Any>` of payment settings "because it's flexible". In your own words, explain what a type parameter or a typed class buys you, using where the error shows up.
explain_back.answer: With `Any`, the compiler accepts any value on the way in, so a wrong value is only caught by the cast on the way out. That cast runs in whatever code reads the setting, maybe much later, and the exception points there instead of at the code that stored the bad value. With a type parameter, or a small class with typed fields, the compiler checks every write against the declared type. The bad write becomes a compile error on the exact line with the bug, and readers need no casts, so they cannot fail with a ClassCastException. The flexibility of `Any` is just the freedom to store the wrong thing.

deeper.body:
Two inference tools are worth knowing.

A **`_` type argument** lets you give some type arguments and infer the rest. If a function has two type parameters and only one can be inferred, write `_` for the one the compiler can work out: `runner.run<CardGateway, _>()`. The Kotlin generics page has the full example.

You can also widen a type **on purpose**. `listOf(1, "a")` infers an intersection type that you cannot name. If you really want a list of anything, say so: `listOf<Any>(1, "a")`. Now the type is `List<Any>` and it reads honestly in code review.

One Java detail: the explicit type argument goes after the dot, `Collections.<String>emptyList()`, and it needs a receiver. Inside the same class you must write `this.<String>helper()` or `MyClass.<String>helper()`. In Java 8 and later you rarely need it, because target typing infers the argument from the variable you assign to.

Finally, Kotlin's `List<Int>` holds `java.lang.Integer` objects, so a list of a million ints costs a million small objects. When that matters, use `IntArray`, which is a real `int[]`.
